In office Qilin was sparing with punishments. His aide Liu Puqing pressed him: "My lord, you hold the imperial tally over a region of the realm yet have not ordered a single execution—how can you inspire awe?"
方夏 here means a region of the Chinese realm (華夏), not the season of summer; 仗節方夏 = holding the imperial tally over a region.

While Qilin held office he was sparing in punishments. His aide Liu Puqing urged Qilin, saying: "My lord, you bear credentials in the height of summer yet have made no executions—how will you display authority?"

While Qilin held office he was sparing in punishments. His aide Liu Puqing urged Qilin, saying: "My lord, you bear credentials over a region of Xia yet have made no executions—how will you display authority?"
方夏 denotes a region of the Chinese realm (Xia), not the height of summer; the seasonal reading is a mistranslation.

At that time the Ministry of Personnel consulted Liu Teng and memorialized an appointment for Teng's younger brother, with a concurrent garrison post in the commandery.
其弟 in context is Liu Teng's younger brother: the Ministry deferred to Teng, the prince rejected the appointment, and Teng therefore bore a grudge (s0091-s0092).
The grief of Wei Yi offering his liver and the night weeping in the court of Qin scarcely compare with ours.
The grief of the retainer who took his lord's liver into his own body in the wilds of Wei, and of the envoy who wept night after night at the court of Qin, scarcely compare with ours.

衞野納肝 means 'in the wilds of Wei, taking in the liver' (the loyal retainer who placed his slain lord's liver in his own body); there is no person named Wei Yi. 秦庭夜哭 alludes to the envoy who wept at the Qin court.
Wei Yi's offering of his liver and the night weeping in the court of Qin—how can the pain of a thousand ages compare?
Taking in the liver in the wilds of Wei and the night weeping in the court of Qin—how can the pain of a thousand ages compare?
衞野 is 'the wilds of Wei', not a personal name 'Wei Yi'.

Earlier Zixi betrothed a woman of the Wang clan as wife for his younger brother—a daughter of his aunt—and she bore two sons.
子熙與弟娉王氏為妻 means Zixi arranged Lady Wang's betrothal as wife for his younger brother (與 = for); 'married his younger brother's wife' reverses the relationship.

The Documents say: 'Rather than put the innocent to death, better to fail to apply the regular law.'
寧失不經 means 'rather be remiss in applying the regular statutes' (i.e., err on the side of leniency); 'err through excess' inverts the sense.

The Documents say: 'Rather than kill the innocent, better to fail the regular law.'
失不經 = to fail to follow the regular (law); 'err in excess' misrenders it.

二八 refers to the sixteen worthies of Yao and Shun's court (two groups of eight, 八元八愷), not 'two assistants' plus 'eight worthies'.

二八 = 'two eights', the sixteen worthies; 'Two Assistants and Eight Worthies' misreads the numeral compound.
